writing.exampleCaption: &self borrows, so the caller keeps ownership.
writing.explanation:
impl blocks attach constructors and methods to the type. The receiver spells out the ownership contract: self consumes the value, &self borrows it for reading, and &mut self borrows it for modification — so a method signature tells you what it will do before you read the body.

A struct groups values that belong to one concept. `Rectangle { width, height }` gives those numbers names, so the caller cannot silently confuse the two positions in a tuple. Choose field types that express the valid domain; unsigned dimensions reject negative values at the type level, though you still need to think about multiplication overflow for very large inputs. Construct one value, print its area, then change only its width to see how the named fields clarify the operation.

An `impl` block puts operations next to the type they describe. An associated function such as `Rectangle::new(width, height)` has no `self` receiver and can validate input during construction. A method such as `area(&self)` borrows an existing rectangle. This means several read-only calls can share the same value. A mutating method uses `&mut self` and requires a mutable receiver; a consuming method uses `self` and leaves the old binding unavailable afterward. The signature is a compact ownership contract for callers.

In the counter practice snippet, `bump(self)` consumes the counter and returns only a number. That could be deliberate for a one-shot conversion, but it is surprising for an operation named "bump." If the goal is to retain and update the counter, use `fn bump(&mut self)` and increment its field; if the goal is to produce a modified copy, return a new `Counter` and name the method accordingly. Decide the desired post-call state first, then choose the receiver. This habit prevents ownership errors from turning into unnecessary clones.

A struct combines fields that belong to one concept. A `User` with `name` and `age` is easier to understand than two unrelated variables passed together through many functions. The field names describe roles; the type groups them into one value. Constructing a struct requires values for every required field unless a constructor or default supplies them. Access a field with dot syntax, and make the binding mutable if you intend to change a field through it.

Trace a value from construction to a function call: which code owns it, which fields are read, and whether it can still be used afterward. Then add a field and follow the compiler errors at each construction site; they show where your data model is used. If a field must never be invalid, consider a constructor that validates it and keeps the raw fields private. A struct gives data a shape, while methods and visibility rules can protect the meaning of that shape.
writing.feedback: &self or &mut self keeps the value usable after the call.
